title: From power-on to login on the Jetson Orin Nano

steps.title: Seven stages, five of them NVIDIA binaries
steps.body:
Read the left column from top to bottom: each card is one stage that starts the next. Each card says which processor runs it and where its code is stored. The orange panel on the right lists extra firmware for the chip's other cores.

The firmware (stages 1 to 5) lives in the module's QSPI-NOR flash, a small boot flash on the module itself. NVIDIA ships it as binaries, so you configure it rather than compile it.

steps.title: The BootROM is silicon and starts everything
steps.body:
The BootROM is code hard-wired into the chip. It runs on the BPMP (the boot and power management processor) as it leaves reset, initializes the QSPI-NOR boot media and loads the first boot images, including MB1.

It also checks signatures: the PSC ROM holds the NVIDIA and OEM keys and authenticates MB1 and PSC-BL1. Because it is mask ROM, software cannot damage it, which is why recovery mode can always work.

steps.title: MB1 sets up the platform and the memory
steps.body:
MB1 (Microboot 1) runs on the BPMP and is stored in `A_mb1`, with its configuration in `A_MB1_BCT` and `A_MEM_BCT`. A BCT is a boot configuration table: board data that the binary reads.

MB1 configures pinmux, GPIO, pad voltages and firewalls, initializes the SDRAM from the Memory BCT, loads the firmware for the CPU complex and sets the PMIC rail for the CPUs. Without it there is no working RAM for anything after it.

steps.anchor: Next-stage bootloader on the CPU complex
steps.title: MB2 is the first code on the Arm cores
steps.body:
MB2 (Microboot 2) is stored in `A_mb2` and runs on the CCPLEX, NVIDIA's name for the CPU complex, the Arm cores that will later run Linux.

The same component also receives images from the host PC when you flash the board, in cold-boot flashing and in RCM boot. That is why the flash flow depends on it.

steps.title: UEFI chooses where the OS comes from
steps.body:
UEFI is the CPU bootloader (CPUBL), stored in `A_cpu-bootloader`, which is 3.5 MiB. It is built on EDK2 and its source is public in NVIDIA/edk2-nvidia.

It applies the `.dtbo` overlays shipped in `kernel/dtb` (`L4TConfiguration`, `BootOrder` and others), picks the boot device from `DefaultBootPriority` and starts the OS loader. The secure OS (OP-TEE) sits next to it in `A_secure-os`, 4 MiB.

steps.title: L4TLauncher loads the kernel named in extlinux.conf
steps.body:
L4TLauncher is UEFI's default OS loader. It is the file `EFI\BOOT\BOOTAA64.efi` on the `esp` (the small FAT partition that UEFI reads).

With the shipped `L4TDefaultBootMode = 1` it loads the kernel, initrd and device tree listed in `/boot/extlinux/extlinux.conf` on the root filesystem. Other modes take the kernel and DTB from the `kernel` and `kernel-dtb` partitions, or start GRUB.

steps.anchor: Gets the device tree and a command line
steps.title: The kernel is the first stage this repository builds
steps.body:
Linux 5.15.148-tegra is read from `/boot/Image` and `/boot/initrd` on the root filesystem. It receives the device tree and a command line with `root=PARTUUID=...`.

The initrd (a small initial RAM filesystem) mounts the real root filesystem from SD, NVMe or USB, then the kernel starts `/sbin/init`, which is systemd. The card's badge says `built by this repo`: `./build.sh` compiles it from NVIDIA's public sources.

steps.title: Userland ends at a login prompt
steps.body:
The last stage is the Ubuntu 22.04 userland on the `APP` partition (ext4), started by systemd. NVIDIA's L4T libraries (core, display, camera, multimedia) sit on top of the Ubuntu base.

First boot ends at a login prompt for the user you created during the build, with no first-boot wizard.

steps.title: Other cores get their own firmware, in two copies
steps.body:
The chip has several processors besides the Arm cores, for example the SPE (sensor processing engine), RCE (camera real-time core), DCE (display engine) and ADSP (audio). Each loads firmware from its own partition such as `A_spe-fw` or `A_dce-fw`, all in QSPI-NOR.

Every partition exists twice, `A_` and `B_`, so there are two complete boot chains and a failed firmware update does not leave the board dead. Names and sizes come from `bootloader/generic/cfg/flash_t234_qspi.xml`.

steps.title: The module holds the firmware, the drive holds the OS
steps.body:
The eMMC-less Orin Nano has no storage of its own except the 64 MiB QSPI-NOR. The firmware always sits there, and the OS lives on the SD card, NVMe or USB drive you attach.

That split is the key difference from SD-card boards, and it is why flashing needs NVIDIA's tools and recovery mode.
